doc.title: Paul Shaffer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 24, 2023

title: Apprenticing with guitarist Michael (Tisziji) Munoz
summary: Munoz taught him standards voicings and Coltrane-like one-chord accompaniment and listening; they are still working together on a new record.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: into a bunch of open-minded musicians there, all of them in the Army, and he became a guitarist of this type that I’d never seen before or since really because he doesn’t play any chords or harmonies or anything, he treats his guitar as if it were a saxophone and he were John Coltrane. And I’m still playing with him today because he and I have both — you know I came to the U.S., he returned to the U.S. after some time in Toronto and we hooked up again here and I’m right in the middle now of doing a record with him now. He’s still so original he now uses a spiritualistic type of first name Tisziji Munoz but the Munoz is still there. He can be heard on YouTube and stuff and this record we’re making together pretty soon. Still you know the most open kind of guy. And after he started me on standards in that little practice room at the dorm then he said, “Okay now we’re not going to play changes at all anymore, just one chord, let’s go.” And he started training me how to kind of accompany him in sort of Coltranesque explorations. And he was kind of strict too this guy. He trained me how to really listen. Listen to him. Play what he’s indicating. If I spaced he could tell immediately, I would hear his frustration. Just [wails] and I knew, I tried to avoid that at all costs. So that was the kind of training I got from this guy and when I started to play with him in the second year I cheered up and I didn’t have to sleep anymore and it was just clear what I had to do.
Oh what a fortuitous 6 AM walk for you.
And something you pointed out, that you were an apprentice, and that idea of having a mentor is not around as much as it used to be so it’s fortunate that that happened for you.

It sure is. And he continues to be a mentor this guy, fascinated by him. Now this latest record that we just recorded and we’re kind of dealing with now at the stage of now how do we finish it exactly. But he’s at the point now where we’ve got two great musicians. He said to me, “Get me, you know, instead of the guys I normally play with, who do you think I should play with?” And so I got the great Will Calhoun on drums who you may know from playing with the group now whose name escapes me. Excuse me? Yes. “Living Colour” spelled the Canadian way, C-O-L-O-U-R. Will Calhoun on drums and he said you’ve got to get Jamaaladeen Tacuma on bass, whom I was already familiar with. These two guys and Tisziji and myself, and Tisziji, there’s no tunes anymore or no even discussion. He just starts to play and we start to play and that’s how this album was done.
